title: Rebuilt NHC 48-hour error circles had higher coverage for forecasts that started as hurricanes in 2017-2025
abstract: We tested the NHC five-year, two-thirds radial track error rule with official 1989-2025 error tables. Radii used earlier years only. At 48 hours in 2017-2025, coverage was 70.3% in the Atlantic and 69.9% in the eastern North Pacific. Coverage was 82.2% and 81.8% for forecasts with initial best-track winds of at least 64 kt, versus 63.4% and 63.2% below 64 kt. Storm bootstrap intervals for the two strength gaps were 11.2-26.1 and 11.4-25.7 percentage points. Equal storm weights retained the gap. Within storms with both strength classes, the late-period differences were smaller and uncertain. Thus, the pooled result does not establish a causal strength effect. A ten-year radius history had worse quantile loss than five years; three years gave no clear gain at 48 hours. Rebuilt 2026 radii differed from the published values by at most 1.7 nautical miles. Revised best-track inputs, excluded storm stages, fixed fitted radii in uncertainty estimates, and lack of historical issued radii limit inference. This is a test of the reconstructed circle rule, not of the full cone or impact risk. Code, aggregate evidence, source hashes, and independent numerical checks support reproduction.

display.caption: Rebuilt five-year error circle coverage in 2017-2025 by lead and initial best-track wind. Bars show storm bootstrap 95% intervals. The dashed line is two-thirds. These circles do not measure full-cone coverage.

citations.reason: Motivates tests of public hazard products; no PAGER observations are reused.
